title: Adopt the Craft, Author the Seam — rich
forward_vector: I am the manifest of Adopt the Craft, Author the Seam's rich face, its first round at Sketch tier, a proposal. For the first seam I gather BLUELINE's round-trip, where the staging vocabulary survived 2D to 3D and back. For the rest I carry the page's claim into music, Loudon's home craft, which it names and never works: a chart read by a drummer and by a machine, walked up to sixteen blind trials asking which take is the drummer; one record written three ways, walked up to two scored rounds asking whether the ear can read it back; and, beside the tension, Loudon's own open reading made playable and left open. One engine runs all three. I grow when a listener's scores come back, and when he answers the question. I never hold the entry's words.
entry: Adopt the Craft, Author the Seam
grain: The page's own ## grain: four sections carry pieces, one each, so each can be approved on its own. The opening section, Forward Vectors and Active Baton carry none.

offers.what: The section names music production and never works it. It could carry one worked line: a chart that says "swing, laid back" goes to a sequencer and comes back straight; the seam is the swing ratio, the lay-back and a lean on 2 and 4. That a default sequencer plays it straight is true without any score, so the gate is Loudon's read, after his answer to the open question the baton carries. The third kind of trial in "which one is the drummer" decides the wording: if listeners score 7 or more of 8 on the leftovers, the line should also name what the record has no field for (ghost notes, the pickup into the turnaround).

Found while making "match it by ear": in music the section's convergence doesn't arrive on its own. A chart says "medium swing, laid back", never 64%; the machine's vocabulary is numbers and the human's is words, so the one vocabulary serving the human read, the machine and the handoff had to be built here. Either convergence is the signal of the right seam only where a craft already writes its vocabulary down (staging does, feel does not), or in music the seam's new work includes making the vocabulary. For Loudon; not settled by the piece.

verdicts.why: A real test of seam 1 (17/3/0, once 11/3/6) that loads its report on the live face; it opens on its summary, but the baton forbids a rebuild and the caption walks up. Note: the residual fixes went to the diff and the metric, not only "the shared rig".

pieces.title: BLUELINE seam A round-trip · animatic → Blender → reprojected, 2026-06-17
pieces.caption: **The first seam, already tested.** Five board records realized in Blender, their keypoints reprojected to 2D, and the authored staging diffed against what came back: facing, shot size, laterality and eyeline. 17 pass, 3 warn, 0 fail, after three passes (11/3/6, then 16/2/2, then 17/3/0): the first fixes went to the shared rig (the camera solver, the head-aim), the last two to the diff (a depth exemption) and to the metric itself, which had been wrong while the aim was right. Amber is the facing the board authored, coral the facing read back from the render; where they coincide, the vocabulary survived the handoff. The three warnings are near-misses on three different dimensions. What it tests is that one vocabulary crosses from 2D to 3D intact. It doesn't render the comic fidelity, and it doesn't write depth back to the record, so those two halves of the section stay untested here. Gathered from BLUELINE as it stands, not rebuilt: the baton says so, and the report beside it is `seam-a-roundtrip-report.md`.

pieces.title: Match it by ear · one record, four readers, up to two scored rounds
pieces.caption: **Can a person recover the numbers from the sound?** The section's sign of the right seam is one vocabulary serving the human read, the machine and the handoff. In music the machine and the handoff read two numbers by construction, so the ear is the part that can be tested, and what it tests is narrower than the section's "human read": whether a listener can recover the numbers from the sound, so the record is no finer than an ear can use, not whether a person reads the record. Step 1 shows the other half honestly: a real chart says *medium swing, laid back*, never a percentage, so in music the shared vocabulary has to be built. Five steps: one groove written as a chart says it, as the machine's instructions and as a file; swing heard alone at three settings; lay-back heard alone; the match-by-ear game from the Daily Page's rough two, which Loudon called a great ear-training quiz, unscored; and last two scored rounds of six, swing then lay-back. Chance is stated before the first trial: a reader who never listens locks in 30% and 33% of trials, and gets 5 or 6 of 6 that way 1.2% and 1.8% of the time. The hidden groove and yours differ only in the one number: same hits, weights, length and loudness (checked headless).

Kind 2 is the seam plus the maker-sized wander, with rough two's ghosts and turnaround pickup removed. Reword kind 1, say kind 2 measures that wander or restore the leftovers as a third kind, state the best non-listener 7.1% (4/56) beside 3.5%, and keep "defaults" marked as the outside read's.

pieces.title: Which one is the drummer? · from the chart to the seam, up to twenty-four blind trials in three kinds
pieces.caption: **The section's claim, carried into music.** A chart that says *swing, laid back*, read by a drummer (as the chart asks, or with rough two's ghost notes and turnaround pickup); the same chart read by a machine, which plays it straight; one number authored (where the skip note lands); then two numbers and a switch (the lay-back, a lean on 2 and 4), the whole record. Last, twenty-four blind trials in three kinds, shuffled. A control: the drummer against the machine as written, whose straightness is built in, so it tests the ear, not the page. The wander: the drummer against the machine reading its own seam; this drummer is that seam plus a wander an agent sized (about 3 ms and 0.7 dB a hit), so this kind asks only whether that wander is heard. The leftovers: the drummer with rough two's ghost notes and turnaround pickup against the same seam, the kind that can go against the two-number record: 7 or more of 8 says the seam is wider than its record. Chance is 4 of 8 a kind; a coin gets 7 or more 3.5% of the time, and because the 4/4 balance is disclosed, the best non-listener 7.1%. Every take's drums are set to one RMS and the bass is the same; nulls show each pair differs in nothing else. The drummer is a model; the real test is a real record.
pieces.near: Find that point; it is your only new work.

verdicts.why: Faithful to the baton as a proposal that plays the question. But its "edge with a zone" is the blur around the breaking point, not Loudon's zone between the norm and the edge: rename it. The coin figures are exact (0.49/10.6/85.4/3.49%), but a level-blind answerer who leans gets sharp 5.8% and zone 12–20%, so give both.

pieces.title: Where it stops being a groove · Loudon's open reading, played, not settled
pieces.caption: **Loudon's open reading, not the page's claim.** In the Daily Page sit of 2026-10-19 he wondered whether authorship lives in the zone between a craft's norm and its breaking point. The page doesn't carry that reading, and this piece doesn't decide it; approving this section approves a piece, not his reading. Four steps: the groove at its norm (64%, 22 ms, leaning on 2 and 4); the swing pushed from straight to limping; the kit dragged back until it comes loose; and last fourteen shuffled takes, seven swing amounts each heard twice, each answered "still a groove" or "it broke". It finds one end of his zone, the breaking point, and says so; the norm end is set at 64%, not measured. The rule is stated first: a sharp edge, a blurred edge, fog, or no edge in the range. Without listening, a coin flipper gets a sharp edge 0.5% of the time and an answerer who leans one way 3.5 to 5.8%; a blurred edge comes 11 to 20% of the time either way, so it says less. What the zone means is his to say.
